item.title: U.S. transportation secretary refuses to apologize for FAA's nationwide ground stop
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
WASHINGTON, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Sunday refused to apologize for Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)'s nationwide ground stop that lasted for hours on Friday, which disrupted over 10,000 flights, with the impact continuing throughout the weekend. "It happened on my watch," Duffy told NBC News' "Meet the Press." "But I can't apologize for what was passed off to us, and I can't blame Republicans or Democrats because it's all of them." The transportation secretary blamed his predecessors and previous administrations for failing to do enough to modernize the U.S. air traffic control system, describing it as "30 years of a lack of investment." Duffy's remarks came two days after the FAA issued a national ground stop that lasted more than four hours, triggering widespread flight cancellations and delays that continued through the weekend. More than 14,000 flights were canceled on Friday and Saturday, according to data from flight-tracking website FlightAware. U.S. media described the incident as the longest nationwide ground stop since the 9/11 terrorist attacks. At a press conference on Saturday, Duffy attributed the disruption to "routine maintenance" at a "remote FAA location," where a contractor identified as L3Harris was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber-optic lines. Duffy has repeatedly urged the U.S. Congress to approve billions of dollars in funding to overhaul the nation's aging air traffic control infrastructure. At the same press conference, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford offered a "sincere apology to the American traveling public" affected by Friday's nationwide ground stop, emphasizing that the decision to pause all flights was made "out of an abundance of caution." Bedford said that U.S. air travel was not expected to return to normal schedules until late Sunday. ■

item.title: Golden pomelo industry sweetens life in south China village
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
GUANGZHOU, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- In early November, south China's Guangdong Province is still warm and lush, with harvest activity in full swing as terraced pomelo orchards in the village of Nanfu in the city of Meizhou bear heavy golden fruit, while growers weave among the trees picking and sorting. Meizhou is China's second-largest pomelo-producing region and the largest in Guangdong, and is known as the "hometown of the Chinese golden pomelo." One in every five pomelos sold in China comes from Meizhou. In 2026, the city's planting area is expected to reach 670,000 mu (around 44,700 hectares), with output exceeding 1.3 million tonnes and full-industry-chain output value approaching 9 billion yuan (about 1.34 billion U.S. dollars). The golden pomelo is becoming a pillar of income growth for local farmers. COOPERATIVES HELP GROWERS SELL SMARTER Meizhou locals have a long tradition of growing pomelos, which are seen as auspicious in local culture and a signature fruit served to guests in autumn and winter. In the past, many growers planted on a small scale and sold alone, often struggling to get good prices for quality fruit or to secure stable buyers. In recent years, local authorities have built platforms and mechanisms to support the entire chain from planting to sales, promoting collective development of the pomelo industry. Yanyang Township in Meixian District of Meizhou is one of the core producing areas, featuring more than 30,000 mu of orchards, output value of nearly 400 million yuan and over 7,000 growers. Nanfu, notably, has set up a pomelo cooperative, with more than 90 percent of growers joining. The cooperative makes bulk purchases of agricultural inputs, organizes training, standardizes orchard management and coordinates sales. Nanfu's pomelo output value now exceeds 57.5 million yuan, with per capita annual income up by 28,800 yuan and pomelos accounting for more than 80 percent of growers' total income. "We used to figure out farming by ourselves, and when selling, we just waited for wholesalers to come and the prices were low. Now experts teach us techniques hands-on and help us find buyers," said Li Yongsheng, head of the Meixian golden pomelo association. Taoyao Township in Meixian runs courses timed to the farming calendar, including a three-day livestreaming workshop ahead of the pomelo season. "My first livestream sold 12 orders in an hour and a half, and 12 more the next day. Now I stream every day, orders keep growing, and I've built up a group of repeat customers," said a trainee named Zhang Xia. E-commerce is cutting out intermediaries and leaving more profit with growers. E-commerce operator Chen Zengli said he and his wife handle sales themselves and have sold over 100,000 jin (roughly 50 tonnes) more pomelos this year than last year. Meizhou has also launched a pomelo tree adoption program, opening 500 trees at 10 premium orchards for adoption. "Adoption is essentially presale. It brings consumers and orchards closer, enhances the experience, locks in sales in advance, and promotes integrated rural tourism," said Yang Jingliang, chairman of Guangdong Runtu Ecological Agriculture Co., Ltd. The industry is attracting growing numbers of young people back to their hometowns. Lin Lyu, a third-generation pomelo grower, has taken over the family orchards and moved to large-scale and standardized operations. "We have 1,700 mu of standard orchards and annual sales of 30 million jin (approximately 15,000 tonnes). We sell through wholesale, e-commerce and exports simultaneously, and many customers in Europe and Australia specifically seek out Meizhou pomelos," he said. TECHNOLOGY BOOSTS QUALITY, EFFICIENCY "I grow more than 400 pomelo trees, and output is on par with last year. The biggest surprise this year is the sweetness. Following the agricultural research institute's guidance, we spread quicklime in the orchards to reduce acidity and increase sugar content," said grower Huang Yuliang from Nanfu. Modern equipment is also boosting quality and efficiency. Hillside rail transporters now move over 350 kg of fruit per trip, and drones carry fruit baskets in the event of steep terrain. Integrated water and fertilizer systems and IoT monitoring devices, meanwhile, enable growers to irrigate and fertilize remotely via their phones. In 2025, the orchard managed by Huang Yuji in Nanfu saw output rise by about 20 percent. "We used to fertilize by feel. Now we go by data, fertilizer costs are down 15 percent, and the sugar content is more stable," he said. Drones have become common in Meizhou's mountain orchards. "Spraying an orchard that would take seven or eight people a week to do can be done by two drones in two nights, and pesticide use has dropped by 30 percent," Yang said. Agricultural technicians are stationed in the fields year-round. The agricultural research institute of Meixian has developed local management plans covering soil improvement, pruning and fruit thinning, and a special harvesting technique to reduce bruising and extend shelf life. "Only when fruit quality improves, can everyone sell in volume and at good prices," said Zhong Yonghui, head of the institute. MORE THAN JUST A POMELO A golden pomelo is valuable from skin to pulp. At the Nanfu golden pomelo base, shelves are lined with processed products such as peel candy, juice, beer and blossom tea. Local businesses are turning a single-season fruit into a diverse product range. "We have developed 40 products so far, extending the sales cycle and raising added value," Li said. Meixian has cultivated six deep-processing companies making products including pomelo tea, wine and naringin. "Fresh fruit is only available in autumn, but processed products sell year-round, making the industry more resilient," said Zhang Weisi, deputy general manager of a local company. Longer supply chains mean more jobs. Villagers find work nearby in orchard management, processing, warehousing and food services. Yang Youyuan earns a steady 5,000 yuan a month as a chef at a pomelo-themed farm restaurant. "I can care for my family here and still earn money," he said. Yanyang Township has developed picking, sightseeing and homestay businesses, attracting tourists year-round. "More self-driving tourists and tour groups come, and they stay to eat and lodge, diversifying villagers' income," said Gu Haihui of the town's economic development office. Meizhou now has 120 pomelo processing companies, shifting from selling fresh fruit to selling products. Exports of the fruit reached 2,605.86 tonnes in 2025, surging 69.1 percent year on year, while reaching more than 20 countries and regions. Meizhou has issued a three-year action plan (2026-2028) focusing on quality, brands, supply chain and incomes, aiming to push the industry's output value past 10 billion yuan and make the golden pomelo a true "golden tree." ■

item.title: Symposium in New York honors Edgar Snow's legacy as bridge builder between China, U.S.
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
by Xinhua writers Shi Chun, Xu Jing and Xie E NEW YORK, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- Scholars and representatives from China and the United States gathered in New York on Saturday for a symposium honoring Edgar Snow, the American journalist whose pioneering reporting helped introduce the Chinese revolution in the 1930s to the world and whose legacy continues to inspire efforts to foster mutual understanding between the two countries. The symposium, themed "The Bridge Builder: Remembering Edgar Snow's Journey 90 Years Ago," brought together nearly 100 participants, including Snow's family members, representatives of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation (USA), and Chinese and U.S. scholars on Snow studies. In 1936, at the age of 31, Snow broke through blockades and ventured deep into China's impoverished northwest to interview the Red Army. His reporting resulted in the groundbreaking book "Red Star Over China." After the founding of the People's Republic of China, he made three reporting trips to the country, opening a new window on "Red China" to the international community. At Saturday's symposium, speakers shared their reflections on Snow's historical contributions and contemporary influences, highlighting the enduring relevance of his efforts to bridge cultural divides and help the world gain a better understanding of China. President of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation Sidne Ward recalled a study tour this summer with Snow's relatives, international representatives and scholars retracing part of Snow's 1936 interview journey in Shaanxi and Ningxia. "It makes me feel more connected to him and to his experiences 90 years ago," she said. For Nancy Hill, president emeritus of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation, Snow has many different legacies as a premier journalist and a bridge builder. "He saw the plight of the Chinese people and cared. And he reported that story with his head but also with his heart. I think that's a really beautiful lesson that people can learn from," Hill said. Sun Hua, director of the China Center for Edgar Snow Studies at Peking University, viewed the pursuit of truth, respect for other cultures and a spirit of dedication as Snow's most precious spiritual legacy. "The reason 'Red Star Over China' has remained enduringly significant for 90 years lies in its authenticity and its unvarnished, first-hand source material. That is truly unparalleled. To this day, it remains one of the most authoritative works on the early history of the CPC," Sun said. ■

item.title: Explainer: APEC comes to Shenzhen: where "China Opportunity 2.0" meets the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
BEIJING, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- Next week, the gaze of the Asia-Pacific will turn to a young metropolis in southern China that, about four decades ago, was little more than a quiet fishing village. Shenzhen will play host to the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting -- the first time in 12 years that China has hosted the top event of the region's highest-level, most extensive and most influential economic cooperation mechanism. China officially joined APEC in 1991. Shenzhen, adjacent to Hong Kong, will become the third Chinese city after Shanghai and Beijing to welcome this gathering. Its rise over the past few decades stands as a miracle in the annals of global development, demonstrating what the Chinese people can achieve. When Shenzhen was designated a special economic zone in 1980, its GDP stood at just 270 million yuan (around 40.2 million U.S. dollars). By 2025, that figure had soared to 3.87 trillion yuan, trailing only Shanghai and Beijing. China's choice of Shenzhen mirrors a pattern common to other APEC economies, which tend to favor national capitals, major economic or technological hubs, or internationally renowned tourist destinations as host cities. For the 2026 APEC "China Year," China has set openness, innovation and cooperation as its three priorities. They echo the very forces that have shaped Shenzhen's development: openness is the city's defining feature, innovation its greatest strength, and cooperation a driving force behind its continued growth. MARKET FOR THE WORLD Shenzhen's rise over more than forty years owes much to China's reform and opening up. One of the country's first special economic zones, Shenzhen has been a city of opportunity from the very beginning, pioneering one move after another. Countless entrepreneurs and innovators have gone there to pursue their ambitions, international investors have established a presence, and Chinese companies such as BYD and Huawei have grown from local businesses into global players. Shenzhen's tale has unfolded in step with the country's opening up. Today, China is expanding high-standard opening up. It has granted zero-tariff treatment to 63 countries, while remaining the world's second-largest importer for 17 consecutive years. In recent years, alongside further opening up the flow of goods, services, capital and talent, China has steadily expanded institutional opening up -- a key hallmark of high-standard opening up -- with respect to rules, regulations, management, and standards. The aim is to build a business environment that is transparent, stable and predictable, and to bring China's institutional framework into closer alignment with international standards. Shenzhen is a core city in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. Under "one country, two systems," the area's distinctive environment of three customs territories and three currencies has created valuable opportunities to explore the alignment of legal rules, cross-border professional practice, mutual recognition of qualifications, streamlined customs clearance and common standards. In this sense, the area serves as a testing ground for bridging different systems and improving institutional connectivity across the Asia-Pacific. INNOVATION DIVIDENDS Today's Shenzhen is internationally known for its technological prowess and is often dubbed "China's Silicon Valley." It now boasts more than 2 million professionals in science and technology. Yet when the special economic zone was first established in 1980, the city's entire pool of technical personnel consisted of just two people: a tractor mechanic and a veterinarian. This contrast captures the scale of Shenzhen's transformation. In recent years, Shenzhen's output of new energy vehicles, industrial robots and civilian drones has maintained double-digit growth for extended periods. The city has also become a popular destination for shoppers and technology enthusiasts looking to scour Huaqiangbei, its famed electronics market, for the latest products and cutting-edge innovations. China's industrial strengths in emerging sectors such as renewable energy and electric vehicles are no accident. They are the result of years of technological accumulation, well-developed industrial supply chains, and the opportunities created by a vast domestic market. If the "China Opportunity 1.0" of the past was largely about offering the world market dividends via China's enormous consumer market and low-cost production factors, today's "China Opportunity 2.0" is about delivering even greater market dividends while generating innovation dividends through technological progress and industrial upgrading. In China, businesses from around the world can quickly find partners to work with across the entire process, from research and development and prototype testing to mass production. Companies can tap into the Chinese market while strengthening their competitiveness in global markets. Seeing these advantages, foreign companies have increasingly moved beyond simply selling their products in China in recent years. Many have also established research and development centers and regional headquarters in the country. In 2025, 14,000 new foreign-invested enterprises were established in China's scientific research and technical services sector, a year-on-year increase of 27.2 percent. COOPERATION FOR SHARED PROSPERITY The ocean connects rather than divides. Linked by the Pacific, the Asia-Pacific is one of the world's most dynamic economic regions, with deeply integrated regional economies and closely interconnected industrial and supply chains. Cooperation underpins the shared prosperity of the Asia-Pacific and is essential to building an Asia-Pacific community. Against a backdrop of rising unilateralism and protectionism, one of China's most important responsibilities as APEC host is to help bring economies back to the path of openness and cooperation. With global challenges -- climate change, food and energy security, demographic shifts and development imbalances -- intertwined and compounding, no single economy can prosper alone. Over the past year, the 2026 APEC "China Year" has produced substantial results. Working with other APEC member economies, China has organized more than 300 APEC meetings and events, which covered a wide range of areas, including trade, tourism, small and medium-sized enterprises, and energy. They helped build consensus on a series of areas for cooperation. Next week in Shenzhen, participating economies are expected to build on that consensus and deliver more practical outcomes in key areas such as trade, connectivity, the digital economy and artificial intelligence. Such progress would provide fresh impetus for economic growth and prosperity across the Asia-Pacific and beyond. ■

item.title: China's search for U.S. airmen lost along Hump Route keeps WWII bonds alive
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
* Chinese and U.S. representatives held a ceremony in southwest China's Chengdu recently to hand over the remains of U.S. airmen who went missing along the Hump Route while helping China fight Japanese aggression during World War II (WWII). * More than 1,000 Chinese and American aircrew members lost their lives along the route. The air corridor across the Himalayas became a vital lifeline for Allied supplies supporting China's resistance against Japanese aggression from 1942 to 1945. * China and the United States have cooperated in searching for American military personnel missing during WWII since the 1970s. At the ceremony, a Chinese official said that China has long supported the search on humanitarian grounds and is willing to continue practical cooperation with the United States in this field. CHENGDU, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- Two Chinese honor guards carried a box containing human remains to a table and carefully set it down. U.S. Chief Warrant Officer Christine Bilas then gently placed a folded American national flag on top of this box. "Bring them home," said U.S. Navy Captain Colin Alexander Eliot, a forensic expert with the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA), as he watched the transfer ceremony at Jianchuan Museum in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, on Tuesday. U.S. Navy Commander Gregory Pavone then lifted the box from the table. Inside the box were eight bone fragments recovered from a glacier more than 5,000 meters above sea level in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. Believed to be the remains of American airmen who went missing while helping China fight Japanese aggression during World War II (WWII), these bone fragments had lain in the mountains for more than 80 years. Their identities have yet to be confirmed. The handover followed three expeditions over more than two years by a Chinese civilian search team, part of a decades-long effort by China and the United States to account for missing American military personnel. THREE TRIPS TO THE GLACIER Cering Qoizha, deputy curator of Jianchuan Museum's branch in Chongqing, southwest China, set out in 2024 to search for wartime aircraft wreckage and human remains in the glaciers of Nyingchi, Xizang. A Tibetan from Sichuan's Garze Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, he enlisted his two elder brothers and several local guides for these expeditions. The first attempt was cut short by a damaged cable crossing over a river. After the crossing was rebuilt, the team returned and found aircraft wreckage. It was not until their third trip that they discovered the bone fragments. The journey took them through forests and swamps, across icy rivers and up steep cliffs, where bears, hidden crevasses and ice holes posed constant dangers. On the glacier, decades of freezing and thawing had left the remains trapped beneath rocks. "We could only lie on the ground and use our hands and branches to turn over the rocks and search carefully," Cering Qoizha recalled. The team eventually recovered eight fragments. He had led an earlier expedition that found American aircrew remains in Xizang in 2015. "The crews of the Hump Route gave their lives to support China's resistance against Japanese aggression and lay alone on the glaciers for decades," Cering Qoizha said. "They were heroes. Bringing them back from the glaciers is something I wanted to do, and something I should do." HUMAN COST OF THE HUMP After Japanese forces occupied Myanmar in 1942 and cut off the Yunnan-Myanmar road, which was China's last major overland supply link to the outside world, China and the United States established air routes connecting the state of Assam in northeastern India with Kunming in southwest China. Known as the Hump Route, this air corridor across the Himalayas became a vital lifeline for Allied supplies supporting China's resistance against Japanese aggression from 1942 to 1945. The route featured snow-covered mountains, deep gorges, glaciers and tropical forests. Violent air currents, low air pressure, hail, freezing weather conditions and attacks by Japanese aircraft made the journey perilous. So many planes crashed along the route that crews came to call it the "Aluminum Trail." More than 1,000 Chinese and American aircrew lost their lives along the route. With the high mountains and glaciers making searches exceptionally difficult, many of their remains have never been recovered. "Every day felt like the last," Chinese pilot Zhou Bing, who flew more than 110 round trips along the route, once recalled. Friends who were together one day could be gone the next, he said. The airlift also depended on the labor and sacrifices of ordinary Chinese people. At Jianchuan Museum, enormous stone rollers weighing between eight and 15 tonnes recall the construction of wartime airfields in Sichuan and Yunnan, both in China's southwest. Without access to modern road rollers, dozens or even hundreds of workers had to pull these heavy stones to prepare runways. Some were injured or killed while working under harsh wartime conditions. Chinese military personnel and civilians also monitored Japanese aircraft movements, providing American forces with information on their numbers, types, altitudes and directions when ground radar coverage was limited. KEEPING THE SEARCH ALIVE For Fan Jianchuan, curator of the privately run Jianchuan Museum, searching for the missing American airmen is a way of repaying a debt of gratitude. "When a country, or a person, faces the greatest danger and hardship, having friends come to help is very important," he said. The museum began searching for wartime aircraft wreckage in Sichuan more than 20 years ago, later extending its expeditions to the remote glaciers of Xizang. "The Hump Route crews deserve to be remembered and thanked forever," Fan said. "In practical terms, that means finding their remains in China and returning them to the American side." China and the United States have cooperated in searching for American military personnel missing during WWII since the 1970s. In 2008, China's Ministry of National Defense and the U.S. Department of Defense signed a memorandum of understanding in Shanghai, establishing a formal mechanism for this work. At Tuesday's ceremony, an official with the general office of the Central Military Commission (CMC) said the joint efforts to recover the remains of missing U.S. servicemen were a testament to the two countries' history of fighting side by side against Japanese fascism during WWII. China has long supported the search on humanitarian grounds and is willing to continue practical cooperation with the United States in this field, the official said, adding that such efforts could contribute positively to building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability. Another official with the Office for International Military Cooperation of the CMC said investigation and joint working teams had conducted surveys and excavations in more than 100 locations across China, drawing support from local governments and residents. As the wartime stories of the Flying Tigers and Hump Route became more widely known, growing numbers of Chinese civilians joined the searches, the official said, citing Jianchuan Museum as a notable example. The official said the expanding involvement of ordinary people echoed the two countries' wartime cooperation and showed that "the hope of China-U.S. relations lies in the people." Pavone also spoke of the longstanding cooperation. "These joint efforts have been going on for decades and are one of the most durable areas of cooperation between our two militaries," he said, thanking the museum, local authorities and Chinese military and diplomatic agencies for their contributions. The remains still await identification. After the remains reach the United States, the DPAA will conduct DNA testing, examine historical evidence, and compare military records. Families will be notified only after identification is confirmed. Following the ceremony, Chinese and U.S. representatives visited the Hall of the Heroes of the Flying Tigers, which commemorates the Flying Tigers and other American servicemen who assisted China during WWII. A wall there bears ceramic portraits of 248 American servicemen. Among the thousands of artifacts on display are personal belongings donated by veterans. One donor was Robert Gruber, an elderly American veteran who visited in 2005 while the exhibition was being prepared. When he learned that the exhibition would showcase items related to WWII American servicemen, he was moved to tears. Gruber died not long after returning to the United States, but his belongings remain on display. They include a portrait of him in his youth in military attire and a cherished photograph of his girlfriend, kept in a frame made from the wreckage of a Japanese aircraft. The exhibition has received more than 10 million visitors over two decades. Among the messages in its guestbooks is one from a Chinese visitor: "May the people of China and the United States remember history and cherish peace." ■ (Video reporters: Xue Chen and Tong Fang; video editors: Wu You, Zhang Mocheng and Li Ziwei)

item.title: From Beijing to Shenzhen: China's push for a more connected, dynamic Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
* The Beijing meeting endorsed a vision of an integrated, innovative, and interconnected Asia-Pacific, calling for closer links in infrastructure, trade, and people-to-people exchanges. Over the past 12 years, China has worked with other APEC economies to advance that vision, expanding cooperation from transport and trade facilitation to digital and green development. * As regional connections have expanded, cooperation has moved beyond trade to encompass technologies and industries that will help shape future growth. At the 2014 Beijing meeting, APEC leaders and representatives endorsed the Accord on Innovative Development, Economic Reform and Growth, highlighting innovation and economic reform as drivers of regional growth. * China's expanding market offers companies from other APEC economies opportunities to reach Chinese consumers and build lasting partnerships, while providing regional partners with much-needed expertise and capital. BEIJING, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, south China, from Nov. 18 to 19, marking the first time in 12 years that China is hosting the APEC meeting, following Beijing in 2014. The Beijing meeting endorsed a vision of an integrated, innovative, and interconnected Asia-Pacific, calling for closer links in infrastructure, trade, and people-to-people exchanges. Over the past 12 years, China has worked with other APEC economies to advance that vision, expanding cooperation from transport and trade facilitation to digital and green development. This year's gathering, to be held under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," will focus on three priority areas identified by China -- openness, innovation, and cooperation -- and is expected to help regional economies deepen economic ties and foster new drivers of growth. ADVANCING CONNECTIVITY At Yantian Port in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, nearly 100 international shipping routes operate each week, 53 of them connecting the port with other APEC economies. The flow of goods through the port reflects the growing connectivity and deepening economic ties between China and the wider region. Connectivity was a priority of China's 2014 APEC host year. At the Beijing meeting, leaders and representatives endorsed China's proposal to establish the APEC Cooperation Network on Green Supply Chain and approved the establishment of its first pilot center in north China's Tianjin. The center officially opened in June 2015 to promote green procurement and supply-chain assessment. The Green Supply Chain Network has grown into a key platform for regional cooperation on green trade. Trade agreements have also translated integration into business opportunities. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), which came into force in 2022, has provided a foundation for deeper cooperation toward prosperity, resilience, and sustainability. RCEP binds ASEAN's 10 members at that time with China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand into the largest free trade zone in the world by population and GDP share. By lowering tariffs and harmonizing trade rules, RCEP is estimated to further boost intra-regional trade significantly and strengthen integrated regional supply chains. Alongside RCEP, the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area (CAFTA) has been significantly upgraded under CAFTA 3.0, which was signed at the 28th ASEAN-China Summit in October 2025. The new version expands the traditional trade pact far beyond tariff reduction. With nine new areas covering the digital economy, green economy and supply chain connectivity, among others, CAFTA 3.0 marks a milestone in economic cooperation that strengthens collective resilience amid global uncertainty. China has also actively promoted infrastructure in the region. Jointly built and operated by China and Laos, the China-Laos Railway links Kunming in southwest China's Yunnan Province with the Lao capital Vientiane, providing landlocked Laos with a rail link to China and access to wider regional markets. Since operation in December 2021, it has carried more than 20.77 million tonnes of import and export goods worth over 100.4 billion yuan (about 15 billion U.S. dollars). The flow goes both ways: durians, mangosteens and other tropical fruits travel north, while Chinese machinery and electronics move south, bringing producers and markets across the region closer together. FOSTERING NEW GROWTH As regional connections have expanded, cooperation has moved beyond trade to encompass technologies and industries that will help shape future growth. At the 2014 Beijing meeting, APEC leaders and representatives endorsed the Accord on Innovative Development, Economic Reform and Growth, highlighting innovation and economic reform as drivers of regional growth. Trade data point to the growing importance of technology in regional economic ties. In 2025, China's high-tech exports to other APEC economies rose 8.1 percent to 4.63 trillion yuan (about 694 billion dollars), according to the General Administration of Customs. Shenzhen's growing AI sector offers a glimpse of the technological capabilities China can bring to regional cooperation. By the end of 2025, the city had more than 2,600 AI enterprises above designated size, with core AI industry revenue of about 220 billion yuan (about 32.97 billion dollars). At APEC business and AI forums in June 2026, participants from 13 APEC economies discussed AI applications and cross-border cooperation, while institutions from China, South Korea, Indonesia and other economies signed agreements on technology commercialization and cross-border industrial parks. Antonio Basilio, director of the APEC Business Advisory Council Secretariat, said China's experience demonstrated the importance of translating technological innovation into practical economic applications, particularly in manufacturing, logistics, agriculture and services. These technological advances are also reflected in Shenzhen's export mix. In 2025, electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries, photovoltaic products, AI-powered products, and medical instruments and equipment together accounted for 25.6 percent of Shenzhen's exports to other APEC economies. Chinese technology and investment are contributing to industrial development across the region. In Malaysia, Chinese battery maker EVE Energy has brought the second phase of its lithium battery plant into operation, the Southeast Asian country's first such large-scale factory. Located in northwestern Malaysia, the facility has an annual production capacity of 680 million cylindrical battery cells. In Thailand, BYD's Rayong plant has an annual production capacity of 150,000 vehicles and employs more than 6,000 people, about 95 percent of them Thai nationals. Mackenzie Lang, CEO of the Australia-China Youth Group, described Shenzhen as "a city everybody across the world now associates with technological innovation and economic development." He expressed hope that this year's APEC meeting would foster stronger regional economic ties and investment. SHARING PROSPERITY China's expanding market offers companies from other APEC economies opportunities to reach Chinese consumers and build lasting partnerships, while providing regional partners with much-needed expertise and capital. Shenzhen's growing economic ties with the region are a snapshot of this broader cooperation. In the first half of 2026, the city's trade with other APEC economies reached 1.98 trillion yuan (about 296.8 billion dollars), up 33 percent year on year, while investment by local enterprises in other APEC members accounted for nearly 60 percent of Shenzhen's total outbound investment. Meanwhile, the China International Import Expo (CIIE), now in its ninth edition, has also provided a platform for companies from other APEC economies to enter the Chinese market. Australian dairy producer Bulla, which has participated in the expo every year since 2019, reached a direct-sourcing agreement with Chinese grocery platform Dingdong Fresh at the 2025 CIIE. Sam Zhang, who oversees international business at Bulla, said the company's exports to China exceeded 10 million Australian dollars (about 7 million dollars) in the financial year ended June 30, 2026. Beyond expanding market access, China has also worked with other APEC economies to promote development cooperation that benefits local communities. In Papua New Guinea, nearly three decades of cooperation with China on Juncao (the herbal plant for growing edible mushrooms) technology have created new income opportunities for rural households. First introduced to the country's Eastern Highlands Province in 1997, the technology has since been promoted through demonstration centers and farmer training programs. With guidance from Chinese agricultural experts, local farmer Zaka Abori began cultivating edible mushrooms in February 2020. China's International Development Cooperation Agency reported in 2022 that she earned an annual income of 15,000 kina (about 4,240 dollars) from mushroom cultivation, about seven times the annual income of most families in the area engaged in coffee and vegetable farming. By March 2025, Juncao and upland rice technologies had been promoted in 20 districts across 10 provinces of Papua New Guinea, with 3,277 people trained. In April 2026, Prime Minister James Marape called for a major expansion of the partnership, citing its contributions to rural livelihoods and agricultural development. Hans Hendrischke, professor of Chinese business and management at the University of Sydney Business School, said APEC's priorities of openness, innovation and cooperation address fundamental challenges facing the Asia-Pacific region, from resisting protectionism and embracing new technologies to developing common rules for cooperation. (Video reporters: Shu Chang, Mao Pengfei; Video editors: Zhang Yichi, Zhang Ning, Zhao Tianlin) ■

item.title: New opportunities in trade, economic cooperation open next chapter in China-Thailand ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
BANGKOK, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- During his official visit to Thailand from Friday to Sunday, Chinese Premier Li Qiang urged both countries to seize opportunities in trade and economic cooperation to elevate bilateral relations to higher levels. With Li's visit to Thailand, the prime ministers of the two countries have exchanged visits within four months, fully demonstrating the high level of bilateral relations. Under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, bilateral ties have gained fresh momentum as the two sides seek to further translate their longstanding friendship into more tangible economic benefits. The close bond between China and Thailand, often described as "China and Thailand are as close as one family," is a unique advantage of bilateral relations, providing stability brought by high-level mutual trust and friendship. Close and regular communication between the leaders of the two countries, along with strong people-to-people ties and cultural affinity, has provided businesses in both countries with a stable and predictable environment for expanding investment and making long-term plans, Li said when attending a symposium with Chinese and Thai entrepreneurs. Such stability is underpinned by institutional cooperation, including mechanisms such as the "2+2" strategic dialogue between foreign and defense ministers and the joint committee on economic and trade cooperation, which help the two countries to further tap cooperation potential in various fields and deliver more tangible results to better benefit the two peoples. Beyond government-level exchanges, exchanges and cooperation in areas such as culture, youth affairs, education and local affairs, have also enhanced mutual understanding and friendship between the two peoples, and strengthened the public foundation of bilateral friendship. Thai Minister of Culture Sabeeda Thaised has described Thailand-China relations as extending far beyond diplomacy into daily traditions, family devotion and shared values, reflecting five decades of formal bilateral relations. Economic figures further illustrate the resilience of bilateral cooperation. China has remained Thailand's largest trading partner for 13 consecutive years, while Thailand is an important trading partner of China within ASEAN countries. Bilateral trade surpassed 153 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, up 14.4 percent year on year. Data released by the Thai Ministry of Commerce in August also showed that China remained Thailand's largest free trade agreement partner in the first half of 2026. The continued growth of economic and trade cooperation despite headwinds is particularly commendable amid the current turbulent international situation, Li noted. Growing connectivity and flourishing innovation cooperation are generating aggregation and empowering effects, driving practical cooperation between the two countries to new heights. At the symposium, the Chinese premier highlighted the steady progress in the construction of the China-Thailand railway, the official opening of China's Pinglu Canal, and the strengthening "soft connectivity" in areas such as trade rules, standards and finance, which facilitated more seamless interaction of the two markets, enabling more enterprises to generate greater economic benefits. During his talks with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, Li called for the alignment of development strategies and accelerating consultations on a new five-year plan for economic and trade cooperation. During his three-day visit, Li urged the two sides to expand cooperation in investment, finance, new energy, semiconductors and artificial intelligence, encouraging Chinese and Thai enterprises to pursue cooperation in high-tech, emerging and cutting-edge fields including electronic information, clean energy and biomedicine to jointly foster and strengthen new business models and new growth drivers. According to Viboon Supakarapongkul, vice chairman of the Thai Chamber of Commerce, Chinese investment inflows into Thailand have accelerated significantly over the past few years, underpinned by deep-rooted cultural and trade ties, robust local supply chains, technology and advanced manufacturing, as well as strong bilateral communication that helps investors navigate the regional market. In his talks with Sophon Zaram, president of Thailand's National Assembly and speaker of the House of Representatives, Li called for stronger collaborative innovation and joint efforts to promote industrial upgrading. At the business symposium, Li urged enterprises to upgrade cooperation from "production collaboration" to "industrial synergy," enhance complementarity and integration in industrial and supply chains, and promote the alignment and mutual recognition of industry standards, to jointly improve competitiveness through more efficient coordination and move up the global value chain. Thailand and China have a solid foundation for cooperation, with the digital economy offering an important avenue for an even closer partnership, said Soontaree Songserm, senior executive vice president of the Big Data Institute in Thailand. Songserm expressed confidence that stronger links between governments, enterprises, universities, research institutions and technology sectors could translate cooperation into more tangible outcomes. Looking ahead, China-Thailand relations and cooperation would extend beyond bilateral exchanges into "regional outreach." By leveraging Thailand's geographic advantages, making good use of policy dividends such as the entry into force of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, the two countries could expand cooperation in third-party markets worldwide to better achieve win-win and multi-win outcomes, Li noted. Against the backdrop of global uncertainties, the Chinese premier added that China is willing to strengthen coordination and cooperation with Thailand under multilateral frameworks, including China-ASEAN, the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation, the United Nations, the World Trade Organization and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, making new contributions to regional stability, development and prosperity, as well as global peace and development. ■

item.title: Xi's article on jointly building Asia-Pacific community with shared future to be published
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
BEIJING, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- An article by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, on jointly building an Asia-Pacific community with a shared future will be published on Monday. The article by Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, will be published in this year's 22nd issue of the Qiushi Journal, a flagship magazine of the CPC Central Committee. It is a compilation of excerpts from Xi's important remarks on the subject made between October 2013 and November 2025. The article stresses that the Asia-Pacific at present is an economic region with the world's greatest growth dynamism and development potential and is widely recognized as an important engine of global economic growth. It calls for sustaining the region's strong development momentum, embracing a future of shared prosperity, and jointly building an Asia-Pacific community with a shared future featuring openness and inclusiveness, innovation-driven growth, greater connectivity and mutually beneficial cooperation. The article points out that the Asia-Pacific should remain the locomotive of economic globalization. Efforts should be made to contribute significantly to the world through more vibrant and resilient Asia-Pacific cooperation, it notes. The article calls for taking the lead in safeguarding peace and stability, and resolving differences and disputes through dialogue and consultation. It emphasizes the need to play a leading role in enhancing openness and connectivity, firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, and advance regional economic integration and the building of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific. The article also urges efforts to lead the way in pursuing win-win cooperation, fostering a pattern of cooperation in which countries support each other's success and achieve common development. It further underlines the importance of taking the lead in pursuing benefits for all and inclusiveness, with efforts to better bridge development gaps, continuously improve people's well-being, and advance common prosperity for all people in the Asia-Pacific. The article stresses that no matter how far China develops, it will remain rooted in the Asia-Pacific, contribute to its development and bring benefits to the region. China will remain committed to the path of peaceful development and pursue a win-win strategy of opening up. While pursuing its own development, China will actively promote common development among Asia-Pacific countries and create more opportunities for people in the region, it states. The article says China stands ready to work with all parties to jointly build an Asia-Pacific community, promote regional growth and prosperity, and advance practical cooperation in areas that include the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, connectivity, the digital economy and artificial intelligence. ■
